course_description:
This course introduces students to the work of William Shakespeare and some of his contemporaries in the early modern period. It considers a range of themes including power and monarchy; the supernatural (including magic and witchcraft) and emerging scepticism; nature and pastoral space; gender and race. Students will also develop their skills in close reading, literary analysis and research techniques, and have an opportunity to examine rare books from the early modern period in the Fryer library.

In exploring the selection of ﾠdramatic texts, we will consider the historical and political circumstances in which these plays were written, aspects of language, character, class, power, and some of the key themes that preoccupied Shakespeare and other early modern dramatists. The focus plays are representative of a range of genres: history, tragedy, comedy, closet drama and romance. The course will give students a solid understanding of drama from the early modern period, and provide them with techniques on how to appreciate and critically analyse early modern literary culture.

In 2026, the course explores four key themes (power and monarchy; the supernatural and scepticism; nature and pastoral space; and gender and race) across the following 9 plays:

· 1 Henry IV (1597) – Shakespeare

· Julius Caesar (1599) - Shakespeare

· Dr Faustus (A-text, 1604) - Marlowe

· The Witch of Edmonton (1621)- Dekker, Ford and Rowley

· A Midsummer Night’s Dream (1600)- Shakespeare

· As You Like It (1599)- Shakespeare

· The Merchant of Venice (1596) – Shakespeare

· The Tragedy of Mariam (1613) - Cary

· The Tempest (1611) – Shakespeare

Students will also have the opportunity to design a creative response to a play (zine, creative journal or scene rewrite) and the option of including their work in an exhibition at the Fryer library at the end of semester.

course_aims: The aims of the course are:

learning_outcomes.description: demonstrate an understanding of early modern drama and specific knowledge of a range of plays that are representative of the early modern period;
interpret and analyse the historical, cultural, literary, and dramatic contexts of early modern plays in critical and creative ways
locate relevant secondary materials for scholarly research on early modern plays, and apply relevant methods and research techniques; and

write and communicate accurately and clearly in relation to early modern drama; apply relevant critical vocabulary and appropriate theoretical terminology; and develop arguments supported by relevant evidence in your research and analysis.

assessment_details.title: Creative Response
assessment_details.category: Creative Production/ Exhibition, Essay/ Critique, Product/ Design, Reflection
assessment_details.task_description: Word Count: 1000 words maximum Instructions : · Part 1: Design a creative response to one of the plays on the course. This can be in the form of a: o Zine (10 pages max); or o Creative journal (10 pages max); or o Rewrite of a scene (750 words max) from a play. Design elements for the zine or creative journal option could include collage, drawn or traced images, and cut and pasted quotations from the play. The creative journal could, for example, reflect on your reading/watching experiences of the play, or be an imagined journal by one of the characters in the play. The rewrite of a scene could imagine the scene from an alternative perspective or from a particular character’s point of view, or adapt the scene to a modern setting or different context. You are encouraged to use your imagination and creative skills in this exercise. At the same time, the response should evidence your knowledge of the play. · Part 2: Reflection on process (300 words): Reflect on your process and experience in designing your creative response. For example, did your creative response lead to some new insights on the play for you? What meanings might a reader/viewer find in your work? Criteria : · Creativity (10 marks) · Reflection on process (10 marks) · Evidence of knowledge of the focus play (5 marks) Submission : Fill in the Creative Response template on BB which will include your reflection on process and photos/scans of the zine/creative journal (if chosen) or scene rewrite. Upload a file to the Turnitin link via the course BB site. The link for submission will become available in the folder the day before the due date. Exhibition : Students will have the opportunity, if they wish, to have their work for the Creative Response included in an exhibition at the Fryer library at the end of semester (details to be confirmed). AI Policy Open Assessment: In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking. Note that: · while this assessment is classified as open assessment, so the use of AI is permissible, your work is more likely to evidence genuine creativity and reflection if the task is not outsourced to AI; · the use of AI may result in errors and fabricated information and sources eg invented quotations. If your assessment submission contains fabricated materials, this is likely to affect your marks in each of the assessment criteria, and your assessment may be submitted for integrity review. · If AI/MT is used, it must be acknowledged on the cover sheet. · To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools. Library Materials and Gen-AI : Students are also reminded that library materials may not be entered into AI technologies without express permission: Policies and guidelines - Library - The University of Queensland “You may not share, re-publish, copy or enter into AI technologies any part of a resource accessed from our online collections unless expressly permitted in the licence terms for that resource” “Except as permitted under each Publisher's terms and conditions of use, you must not: Use UQ Library resource content as an input to generative AI products or services”. assessment_details.title: Research Essay
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment component will involve undertaking a research project and evidencing the scaffolding of your research process as well as the final product. Students may develop their own research topic on 1 or 2 plays from the course (it can be on the play chosen for the Creative Response). The topic should engage with an aspect of at least one of the 4 themes of the course: power and monarchy; the supernatural; nature and pastoral space; gender and race. The Research Essay will comprise: · an abstract (250 words), · a scaffolding portfolio (3 handwritten pages – scans/photos to be included in the portfolio), comprising: a character map/s, mind map of the research topic and 1 page draft outline); and · the final research essay (1500 words). This should include a Works Cited list that includes any course readings relevant to your topic as well as at least 3 scholarly secondary sources that you have found yourself via the MLA International Bibliography (via the UQ Library). MLA style should be used for the abstract and final research essay. See the online guide OWL MLA. https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_formatting_and_style_guide.html Criteria: · Abstract: clear and coherent outline of the research essay including key data and signposting (5 marks) · Scaffolding portfolio: evidencing aspects of the research process and exploring ideas (10 marks) · Analysis and Argument, supported by quotations from the play/s (10 marks) · Use of scholarly secondary sources (10 marks) · Presentation and Writing (10 marks) Submission : Fill in the Research Essay template on BB which will comprise: a cover sheet; the abstract; scaffolding portfolio (photos/scans of the 3 handwritten pages); and the final essay. Upload a file to the Turnitin link via the course BB site. The link for submission will become available in the folder the day before the due date. AI Policy Open Assessment: In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking. Note that: · while this assessment is classified as open assessment, so the use of AI is permissible, students should be aware that the use of AI may result in errors and fabricated information and sources eg non-existent quotations or invented secondary materials. If your assessment submission contains fabricated materials, this is likely to affect your marks in each of the assessment criteria, and your assessment may be submitted for integrity review. · If AI/MT is used, it must be acknowledged on the cover sheet and referenced in the Works Cited list. · To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools. learning_activities.topic: Week 1: Introduction Lecture 1: Introduction to Shakespeare and the early modern world; course and assessment requirements. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Week 1: No Tutorials
Week 2: Henry IV Part 1 Lecture 2: Henry IV Part 1 (1597) – Shakespeare Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Week 2: Henry IV Part 1 Tutorial 1: Discussion of Henry IV Part 1 and Shakespeare’s early modern contexts; small group activities; writing exercise. Bring to class : your copy of the play; your completed/attempted worksheet; and pen and paper for the writing exercise. Set readings: Required: · Henry IV Part 1 (estimated reading time 2.5-3 hrs) · Garber chapter on Henry IV Part 1 Gaber, Marjorie Shakespeare After All. Anchor Books, 2005. Available online: Shakespeare after All - University of Queensland (uq.edu.au) (1 hr) Recommended: · Bladen, Victoria Henry IV Part 1 Insight Publications, 2012. Henry IV. Part 1 : William Shakespeare / Victoria Bladen - University of Queensland (uq.edu.au) [Library: PR2810 .B63 2012] Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

Week 3: No lecture-Reading Week No lecture or tutorials due to public holiday . Reading : it is recommended that you use this first reading week to read ahead; aim to get through 2 of the course set texts this week (estimated reading time 5-6 hrs). Learning outcomes: L02, L03

Week 3: No Tutorial-Reading Week No lecture or tutorials due to public holiday . Reading : it is recommended that you use this first reading week to read ahead; aim to get through 2 of the course set texts this week (estimated reading time 5-6 hrs).
Week 4: Shakespeare and Rome Lecture 3: Guest lecture by Prof Maddalena Pennacchia (University of Roma Tre, Italy) – Shakespeare and Rome Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Week 4: Julius Caesar Tutorial 2: Discussion of Julius Caesar ; small group activities; writing exercise. Bring to class : your copy of the play; your completed/attempted worksheet; and pen and paper for the writing exercise. Set readings: Required: · Julius Caesar (1599) ( estimated reading time 2.5-3 hrs ) · Garber chapter on Julius Caesar. Gaber, Marjorie Shakespeare After All. Anchor Books, 2005. Available online: Shakespeare after All - University of Queensland (uq.edu.au) (1 hr) Recommended: · Bladen, Victoria Julius Caesar Insight Publications, 2011. [Library: PR2808 .B63 2011] Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
